notes: Naval court martial Article 6 appeal following Grieves; conviction quashed and remedial Order context is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Naval court martial unfair trial under Article 6 after Grieves
key_facts: The appellant was convicted at a naval court martial in July 2003 of using violence to a superior officer and sentenced to 36 days detention.
The Judge Advocate at trial was a serving naval officer appointed by the Chief Naval Judge Advocate, not a civilian.
Following the ECtHR decision in Grieves, the appeal challenged whether Article 6 required an independent and impartial tribunal.
Post-Grieves reforms included civilian Judge Advocates and the 2004 Remedial Order changing appointment procedures.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) on Article 6 fairness and unsafe conviction after leave was granted.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed as unsafe; no re-trial ordered; declaration of incompatibility refused.
enrichment.ratio: Applying Grieves, a naval court martial with a serving naval officer as Judge Advocate appointed by a serving naval officer lacked the independence required by Article 6; where unfairness arises from want of tribunal independence, the conviction cannot be safe.
legal_issues: Whether Grieves applied to naval courts martial after QRRN 3630 and revised briefing notes
Whether Article 6 was breached by court martial composition apart from the Judge Advocate
Whether an Article 6 breach from lack of independence could nonetheless leave a conviction safe
Whether a declaration of incompatibility was warranted under section 53C(4) NDA 1957

Millar v Dickson [2002] 1 WLR 1615

notes: Portuguese bankruptcy recognition and appellant standing; procedural history is complex but the court's conclusions are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Portuguese bankruptcy bars bankrupt from pursuing civil appeals
key_facts: Dr Vakil owed Mr Swycher over £1.5 million following High Court judgments in debt proceedings.
A Portuguese bankruptcy declaration was made against Dr Vakil in Lisbon on 3 July 2000 while embargos proceedings were pending.
The Court of Appeal remitted the question of Dr Vakil's standing to prosecute appeals to Mr Justice Simon, who held he had no standing.
Dr Vakil failed to appear at the permission hearing after repeated adjournment applications and travel to Brazil.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Directions judgment on permission to appeal from Simon J's standing ruling and application to strike out pending appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; appeals 2002/1050 and 2002/1582 struck out for lack of standing; Swycher confirmed in his judgment.
enrichment.ratio: English conflict rules recognise a foreign bankruptcy order in rem notwithstanding pending annulment or appeal; under Portuguese law the bankrupt loses the right to litigate and the trustee takes over, so Dr Vakil had no standing to pursue the appeals.
legal_issues: Whether the Portuguese bankruptcy declaration was final and conclusive for recognition purposes
Effect of pending embargos and recurso on recognition under Dicey Rule 35
Whether Dr Vakil had standing to apply for permission to appeal Simon J's order
Whether non-payment of judgment sums justified striking out the appeals
linked_authorities: Nuvion v Freeman [1889] 15 AC 1

confidence.notes: Conflict of laws analysis and standing outcome are well reasoned. Some procedural history is lengthy but does not affect core holdings.

notes: First SIAC success under ATCSA 2001; permission to appeal refused on perversity grounds; closed material limits open-judgment detail.

enrichment.short_title: Secretary of State refused permission to appeal first SIAC certification cancellation
key_facts: M, a Libyan national, was certified under section 21 ATCSA 2001 as a suspected international terrorist and detained.
SIAC allowed M's appeal in March 2004, the first successful challenge to certification under the 2001 Act.
SIAC found assessments were not reliably supported by evidence and reasonable suspicion of Al Qa'ida links was not established.
Special advocates rigorously tested closed material; M did not participate in the closed hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal on questions of law from SIAC's first cancellation of a section 21 certificate.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; SIAC's decision was not perverse or unsupported by evidence.
enrichment.ratio: SIAC must make its own objective judgment whether reasonable grounds exist for the Secretary of State's belief or suspicion; where SIAC's value judgment on the whole evidence is not perverse, the Court of Appeal cannot interfere on a question of law alone.
legal_issues: Whether SIAC failed to consider the evidence as a whole
Whether reasonable suspicion of links to Al Qa'ida was established
The proper test under section 25 ATCSA 2001
Role of special advocates in closed SIAC proceedings
linked_authorities: Chahal v UK (1996) 23 EHRR 413

notes: Leading interim ASBO without-notice appeal; Article 6 and Rule 5 analysis is comprehensive and outcome clear.

enrichment.short_title: Interim ASBO without notice held compatible with Article 6
key_facts: Leeds City Council and police sought interim ASBOs without notice against 66 individuals linked to drug dealing in Little London, Leeds.
M, aged 17, received an interim order on 2 September 2003 excluding him from the area and restricting contact with named associates.
Owen J refused judicial review but granted Kenny relief on insufficient evidence; M appealed on Article 6 and Rule 5 grounds.
Operation Cape involved daily drug-related anti-social behaviour and fear of witness intimidation if notice were given.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Administrative Court refusal of judicial review of interim ASBO made without notice under Rule 5 of the 2002 ASBO Rules.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; interim ASBO without-notice procedure held lawful; Article 6 not engaged on making of interim order; correct 'just' test applied.
enrichment.ratio: An interim ASBO made without notice for a fixed period with safeguards (service, return date, Rule 6 variation/discharge) does not determine civil rights for Article 6 purposes; the statutory test is whether it is just to make the order, not proof of an extremely strong prima facie case.
legal_issues: Whether Article 6(1) applies to interim ASBOs made without notice
Lawfulness of Rule 5 Magistrates' Courts (Anti-Social Behaviour) Rules 2002
Proper test for granting interim ASBO without notice
Whether without-notice procedure was necessary in M's case

notes: Consent quashing of PCA dispensation with contested abuse-of-process argument rejected; straightforward administrative outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Police complaint investigation dispensation quashed by consent
key_facts: The claimant complained that Merseyside Police assaulted him while in custody after arrest for preaching near St George's Hall, Liverpool.
Investigation was delayed when the claimant absconded from bail; the Police Complaints Authority dispensed with investigation on 10 June 2003.
The claimant was returned to Liverpool on 13 June 2003 and sought reopening of the investigation.
The PCA consented to quashing its dispensation decision; Merseyside Police contested jurisdiction and abuse of process.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review application for quashing of PCA dispensation from investigating a police complaint, heard on consent terms.
enrichment.outcome: Consent order approved quashing the 10 June 2003 dispensation; Merseyside Police ordered to pay claimant's costs against them; investigation to resume.
enrichment.ratio: The Police Complaints Authority has power to review and revoke a dispensation under the 1985 Regulations; quashing the dispensation was proper where the complainant was now available to assist and no prejudice to officers had yet occurred.
legal_issues: Whether the PCA had power to revoke a dispensation once granted
Whether continuing the investigation would be an abuse of process
Whether the court could approve a consent order quashing the PCA decision

notes: Rome Convention Article 3.3 and French banking law analysis is detailed; judgment for Caterpillar on loan enforcement.

enrichment.short_title: English law governs cross-border Caterpillar loan despite French borrower
key_facts: Caterpillar, a Delaware lender, advanced €5.3 million to French SNC borrower SNC Passion to finance construction of MV Passion catamaran ferry.
The loan was governed by English law with English jurisdiction; repayments defaulted from late 2001.
Defendant argued the loan was void under mandatory French banking law as Caterpillar was not an authorised French credit institution.
The transaction involved Singapore shipbuilding, US lender, UK-arranged finance, and Guadeloupe-based borrower.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of loan enforcement claim with illegality defence under Rome Convention Article 3(3) and French banking law.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Caterpillar on loan principal, interest, late charges and arrest indemnity; Article 3(3) inapplicable; French banking law not mandatory.
enrichment.ratio: Article 3(3) Rome Convention applies only where all elements relevant to the situation apart from the choice of law are connected with one country; an international commercial loan with US lender, Singapore build, and multi-jurisdictional performance is not a wholly domestic French transaction.
legal_issues: Whether Article 3(3) Rome Convention prevented choice of English law
Whether French Law 84-46 and CMF provisions rendered the loan illegal
Whether Article 7(1) required application of French mandatory rules
Consequences of invalidity and restitution under English and French law

notes: CCRC reference on improper judge's chambers plea discussions; conviction quashed applying Nazham principles.

enrichment.short_title: Unsafe conviction after improper judge's chambers plea indication
key_facts: The appellant pleaded guilty on rearraignment to section 4 threatening behaviour as an alternative to affray at Butlins Pwllheli.
After co-accused Craggs agreed to give Queen's evidence, the judge indicated in chambers that a section 4 plea would avoid custody.
Counsel's contemporaneous advice recorded clear instructions to fight affray until the judge's second indication created a stark custodial risk.
The CCRC referred the case despite no prior appeal; counsel confirmed the plea was entered after deliberation with his girlfriend.
enrichment.procedural_posture: CCRC reference to Court of Appeal on whether guilty plea was nullity due to improper judicial indication in chambers.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; section 4 conviction quashed as unsafe; no recovery of defence costs.
enrichment.ratio: Improper discussions in the judge's chambers linking plea to sentence created improper pressure; applying Nazham, where such irregularity causally affected the change of plea the conviction is unsafe.
legal_issues: Whether chambers plea and sentence discussions rendered the plea equivocal or involuntary
Causation between judicial irregularity and the appellant's change of plea
Application of principles in Nazham and Nazham
Whether oral evidence should be heard on the CCRC reference

notes: Companion to M ASBO appeal; permission refused on delay, alternative remedies, and merits on infant best interests.

enrichment.short_title: Child's interim ASBO judicial review refused for delay and remedies
key_facts: A, aged 16, received an interim ASBO in Operation Cape on 2 September 2003 and a renewed order on 11 December 2003.
He did not attend return dates or seek variation until after arrest for alleged breach on 6 November 2003.
Owen J in Kenny and M held infant best interests are a primary consideration but dismissed M's claim on evidence; Court of Appeal later upheld M on Article 6.
On renewal the District Judge expressly applied the infant best interests principle per Owen J's judgment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited application for permission and judicial review of interim ASBOs against a child in Operation Cape, Leeds.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused for both orders on delay and alternative remedies; on merits, no error shown in applying infant best interests on renewal.
enrichment.ratio: Delay and availability of Crown Court appeal and magistrates' court variation/discharge make judicial review inappropriate where the alleged error is misapplication of legal test rather than procedural unfairness; best interests of the child are a primary but not exclusive consideration.
legal_issues: Whether delay barred judicial review of the first interim order
Whether Crown Court appeal or Rule 6 application were adequate alternative remedies
Whether the District Judge failed to treat A's best interests as a primary consideration
Relationship between infant best interests and public protection under ASBO regime

notes: Detailed guidance on replaying child witness video evidence to jury; appeal dismissed with Rawlings principles applied.

enrichment.short_title: Jury replay of child witness videos held fair and within discretion

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: The appellant was convicted of four counts of indecent assault on a 9-year-old family friend after majority verdicts.
Five minutes into deliberations the jury requested replay of video-recorded evidence of the complainant and her brother.
The judge replayed both videos in open court and gave balancing directions mid-replay and next day on cross-examination.
Defence counsel acquiesced and did not seek discharge; judge consulted Archbold after replay had partially started.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction on discretionary replay of child witness video evidence after jury retirement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction held safe; discretion properly exercised with adequate balancing directions.
enrichment.ratio: Where a jury requests replay of video-recorded child evidence to assess how rather than what was said, the judge may permit replay with balancing directions under Rawlings; the discretion extends to supporting child witnesses, not only the complainant.
legal_issues: Whether the judge should have refused the jury's replay request
Whether balancing directions were given too late
Whether the brother's video should have been replayed separately
Whether public hostility in court required a direction on emotion

notes: Privilege and administrative receivers' powers over solicitor files; appeals allowed on confidence not waived by unauthorised disclosure.

enrichment.short_title: Receivers exceeded powers passing privileged files to debenture holder
key_facts: GE Capital sought to enforce Paul Sutton's guarantee of Anglo Petroleum Ltd debts after fictitious factored transactions were discovered.
APL receivers obtained Boyes Turner solicitor files under section 234-236 and immediately forwarded them to GE's solicitors without review.
Sutton raised non-disclosure of fake Sutton Oil transactions as a defence; GE sought BT meeting notes from 14 September 2001.
APL, acting through its director Richard Sutton, and Sutton sought injunctions restraining use of allegedly privileged material.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals from refusal of interlocutory injunctions in linked guarantee enforcement and document-return proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals allowed; privilege/confidence not waived by unauthorised disclosure to GE; APL action properly brought by director.
enrichment.ratio: Administrative receivers exceeded their powers in passing privileged BT documents to the debenture holder without considering APL's interests; unauthorised disclosure cannot waive legal professional privilege, and a company director may bring proceedings to protect charged assets where the debenture holder's interests are not prejudiced.
legal_issues: Whether APL's privilege was waived when receivers sent BT files to GE's solicitors
Whether receivers acted within debenture and Insolvency Act powers
Whether Paul Sutton had common interest or personal privilege in BT documents
Whether APL proceedings brought by director without receivers' consent were valid
